title: URL Shortener
summary: Design a public link-shortening service that turns long URLs into short codes, redirects billions of clicks a month with very low latency, and reports click counts to link owners.
statement:
You are designing **a public URL-shortening service** — the kind of short links people put in social posts, SMS campaigns and printed QR codes.

**Users**
- *Anyone* can paste a long URL and get back a short link such as `https://sho.rt/aZ3kQ9x`.
- *Registered users* can also pick a custom alias (`sho.rt/summer-sale`), set an expiry date, list the links they created, disable a link and see how many times each link was clicked.
- *Visitors* simply open a short link and expect to land on the destination page almost instantly.

**Core journeys**
1. **Shorten** — submit a long URL (up to 2,048 characters), optionally with a custom alias and an expiry, and receive the short link.
2. **Redirect** — opening a short link sends the browser to the original URL. Expired, disabled or unknown codes show a "link not found" page.
3. **Stats** — the owner sees total clicks per link and clicks per day for the last 30 days. Counts may lag by a few minutes.

**Clarifications from the interviewer**
- Generated codes are at most 7 characters from `[A-Za-z0-9]`. Custom aliases are 4–30 characters and are first come, first served.
- Codes must not be predictable: nobody should be able to walk through every link by incrementing a code.
- Shortening the same long URL twice may return two different short links; that is fine.
- A link's destination cannot be edited after creation — owners can only disable or delete it.
- Links without an explicit expiry live for 5 years.
- Redirect traffic is extremely skewed: a link shared by a celebrity can receive thousands of clicks per second for an hour, while most links are clicked only a handful of times ever.

Walk through requirements, estimates, APIs, the data model and a high-level architecture, then go deep on the parts you think are hardest.
scaleHints: 100M new short links per month (~40 creations/s on average, ~200/s at peak)
Read:write ratio about 100:1 → ~10B redirects per month (~4K/s on average, ~20K/s at peak); a single viral link can reach 10K/s on its own
Links live 5 years by default → plan for ~6B stored links at roughly 500 bytes each (~3 TB)
Redirect p99 latency under 50 ms measured at our servers; link creation p99 under 300 ms
Click statistics may lag real time by up to 5 minutes
constraints: Redirects must be highly available (99.99%); link creation can tolerate slightly lower availability (99.9%)
A short code, once issued, is never reassigned to a different destination — not even after the link expires
Two different links must never end up with the same code or alias, even when created at the same instant
Generated codes must not be sequential or otherwise enumerable
outOfScope: Detecting malicious or phishing destination URLs
Detailed analytics beyond click counts (geography, referrers, devices)
Billing, paid plans and team accounts
Link previews and QR code generation

keyFunctionalRequirements: Create a short link for a long URL and return it; validate the URL format and length
Optional custom alias with an atomic uniqueness check that rejects taken aliases
Redirect a code to its destination with an HTTP redirect; 404 page for unknown, expired or disabled codes
Optional per-link expiry with a 5-year default lifetime
Owners can list (paginated), disable and delete their links
Per-link click counts (total and daily for 30 days) with a few minutes of lag acceptable
keyNonFunctionalRequirements: Very low redirect latency (p99 < 50 ms server-side) — every click waits on it
Redirect availability of 99.99%; the read path matters more than the write path
Read-heavy (~100:1): ~20K redirects/s at peak plus hot-key spikes on viral links
Durability: a created mapping is never lost or silently changed
Code uniqueness under concurrent creation and non-enumerable codes
~6B links (~3 TB) growing linearly; analytics must never slow down redirects
coreEntities: Link: short_code (PK), long_url, owner_id (nullable), created_at, expires_at, status (active/disabled/deleted)
ClickEvent (transient): short_code, timestamp — consumed by the stats pipeline, not stored per click long-term
LinkDailyStats: short_code, date, click_count — pre-aggregated for the owner dashboard
Code range allocation (if counter-based): range_start, range_end, assigned_node
keyComponents: Stateless API service for creating and managing links, horizontally scaled
Redirect path kept lean and isolated from (or prioritised over) management APIs
Short-code generator: pre-allocated counter ranges plus scrambling, or random codes with insert-if-absent
Key-value style mapping store (code → URL), partitioned by code and replicated
Read-through cache for hot codes, including negative caching of unknown codes
Asynchronous click-event pipeline that batches events into aggregated counts
Background job that expires/purges links and invalidates cached entries
deepDiveTopics: Code generation: base62 counter with per-node range allocation vs random 7-char codes with conditional insert vs hashing the URL; collisions and non-enumerability (e.g. scrambling the counter)
301 vs 302/307 redirects: browser caching vs accurate click counts and the ability to disable links later
Caching hot links: sizing (e.g. top 20% of daily codes), TTLs, invalidation on disable/delete/expiry, a single viral key
Counting clicks without slowing redirects: fire-and-forget events, batching, approximate vs exact counts
Partitioning and replicating ~6B mappings; why the access pattern is a pure key lookup
commonPitfalls: Truncating an MD5/SHA hash of the URL to 7 characters without handling collisions
A single auto-increment database counter: a bottleneck, a single point of failure and trivially enumerable codes
Writing click counts to the database synchronously on every redirect
Choosing permanent (301) redirects while promising accurate stats and the ability to disable links
Skipping estimates, so storage and cache sizes are never justified
Checking a custom alias with read-then-write instead of an atomic conditional insert
